checked_and_fine: cross_tail_mean_q75 (partura/ops_ext.py:313, logic lives in the shared _tail_mean helper at :293-300) matches its docstring: 'mean of the values at or above the 75% quantile of the last d trading days (today included); NaN with fewer than 2 finite days.' Verified element-wise against an independent from-scratch numpy reference (built only from the docstring: per-stock sliding window, np.quantile(...,0.75,method='linear'), filter >= threshold, mean) across 12 (D,S,d) configs x 10 adversarial input patterns (random; 10%/30% NaN; a fully-NaN day; a fully-NaN stock; constant; 3- and 4-distinct-value ties; 1e9/1e16 and 1e-9 magnitude; mixed sign) x float32/float64 = 240 scenarios, plus D<d short-history configs (D=1,2,3 with d=10) and d=1 degenerate windows. The only mismatches found (<=3e-8 absolute, on one deliberately pathological exact-tie pattern -2,-2/3,2/3,2 whose float32 rounding makes 2.0 and 3x(2/3) not quite cancel) were confirmed bit-identical to torch's own float32 .mean()/.sum() on the same values, i.e. float32 summation-order noise inherent to any implementation, not a kernel defect; it disappears entirely in float64 and does not occur in any other tested pattern. Causality verified directly: replacing every day strictly after a cut day t0 with unrelated/extreme-magnitude/NaN values leaves every output on or before t0 bit-identical, across 6 random trials x 2 dtypes. Hand-verified on window=[1,2,3,4,5], d=3: kernel returns [NaN, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0], exactly matching manual quantile-by-hand computation.

The docstring's own explicit claim 'every stock keeps a distinct value (no NaN, no ties)' holds as a mathematical consequence of _pct_rank's bijective (stable double-argsort) rank construction -- the shifted and unshifted output ranges (1,2] and (0,1] cannot collide -- confirmed both by direct analysis and empirically across 11 (D,S) shapes x 10 adversarial input patterns x 2 dtypes (zero violations in the 'no ties among valid stocks' property check). findings.title: cross_tail_mean_q75's docstring never names its quantile convention
findings.summary: The docstring 'mean of the values at or above the 75% quantile of the last d days' never states which quantile estimator is meant; the code (shared _tail_mean, line 297) uses linear-interpolation quantile (torch.nanquantile's default), one of several standard conventions a reader cannot recover from the text alone, even though the module's own rule is 'the docstring of each kernel is its definition.'
findings.evidence: Verified by direct test: torch tensor x=[1,2,3,4] (one stock, d=4) -> ops_ext.cross_tail_mean_q75 returns exactly 4.0.
findings.failure_scenario: Not a bug in the current code (it is internally self-consistent and the convention used -- linear interpolation -- is the common default). But it is a real ambiguity for anyone re-deriving the operator from the docstring alone: window=[1,2,3,4] (4 finite days, no ties). Linear interpolation puts the 75% cutoff at 3.25 (between the 3rd and 4th order statistics), so only the value 4 clears it -> mean 4.0 (this is what the kernel returns). A reader who instead used the 'lower'-interpolation convention (cutoff = the largest sample at or below the true quantile, i.e. 3) would select {3,4} -> mean 3.5. Both are defensible readings of 'the 75% quantile' as worded; the docstring does not disambiguate them.
findings.suggested_fix: Append the convention to the docstring, e.g. '(quantile via linear interpolation between order statistics, i.e. torch.nanquantile's default)', on cross_tail_mean_q75 (lines 313-316) and its sibling cross_tail_mean_q25 (lines 304-309), since both delegate to the same _tail_mean quantile call at line 297.

findings.title: cs_first_low40/high40 and cs_last_high20/low20 don't document the x-bucket's tie-break or rounding
findings.summary: The four docstrings (lines 328, 340, 346, 354) say e.g. 'every stock in the LOWEST 40% of x' but never state (a) how ties in x are broken when deciding bucket membership, or (b) how the cutoff rounds when the valid-stock count isn't an exact multiple of the named percentage -- both are real choices made inside the shared _lexi/_pct_rank helpers (lines 319-324, 224-228) that the per-operator docstrings don't surface.
findings.evidence: Verified by direct test: x=[1,1,1,1,1] (constant, all tied), y=[10,20,30,40,50] -> ops_ext.cs_first_low40 returns [1.2, 1.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0].
findings.failure_scenario: Not an implementation inconsistency (the code is internally consistent and the tie-break matches the project-wide convention documented in alphacube/operators/common.py's own rank(), 'ties keep index order') -- but it is unrecoverable from these four docstrings alone. With x constant across all 5 stocks that day (x carries no information about which stocks are 'lowest'), cs_first_low40 still places the stocks at column positions 0 and 1 into the 'LOWEST 40% of x' bucket (+1 boost) purely because of their position in the input array: output = [1.2, 1.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0]. Separately, for a valid-stock count not divisible by the named fraction (e.g. 7 valid stocks), 'lowest 40%' actually selects floor(0.4*7)=2 of 7 = 28.6% of the names, not 40%, because the bucket is an integer-rank cutoff (rank<=floor(pct*n)).
findings.suggested_fix: Add one sentence to _lexi's docstring (line 319-320), inherited by all four callers, stating the tie-break rule (ties in x and y are broken by column/stock order, matching common.rank's documented convention) and that a bucket's actual share can differ from its name when the valid-stock count isn't an exact multiple of the percentage.
